solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Doctor is not late at bar — he never drinks!

indicators.note: to doctor something is to tamper with it, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: the fourteen letters rearranged

explanation.surface: A man drinking at the bar claims he is not late, yet insists he never touches alcohol.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Doctor' is a verb here, the anagram signal acting on IS NOT LATE AT BAR.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who abstains completely from alcohol is described as one who never drinks.

clue.text: They should attract young and old, for instance

definitions.meaning: the saying goes that unlike things pull towards each other
pairs of contrary words, such as young versus old

explanation.surface: A matchmaker hopes people of different ages will be drawn to one another.
explanation.definitionFit: The proverb says contrasting things attract, and young and old are an example of contrary terms.

clue.text: Change brought about by Raleigh's beheading

indicators.note: removing the head means the first letter of the name goes

parts.note: Sir Walter Raleigh, the Elizabethan courtier, who was himself executed by beheading

explanation.surface: Something altered by the execution of Sir Walter Raleigh.
explanation.walkthrough: Raleigh was beheaded in 1618, so the surface is historical; 'beheading' drops the W of WALTER.
explanation.definitionFit: To change something is to modify or vary it, a plain synonym.

clue.text: Husband affected by wanderlust you could say

definitions.text: Husband affected by wanderlust you could say

parts.words: Husband affected by wanderlust you could say
parts.note: read 'wanderlust' as lust that wanders, i.e. a married man whose desire strays beyond his wife

explanation.surface: A husband with an urge to travel the world.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wanderlust' suggests travel, but split it as wandering lust and the husband is unfaithful.
explanation.definitionFit: A married man whose desires stray from his spouse is an unfaithful partner.

clue.text: Southern Region introduces decoration on the wagon

indicators.note: the railway region takes the honour into its middle, letting it in

parts.note: SR was British Rail's Southern Region
the OBE, Order of the British Empire, is a British honour

explanation.surface: A railway region hands out an award to someone who has given up drink.
explanation.walkthrough: SR was the Southern Region of British Railways; 'on the wagon' is an idiom for abstaining from alcohol.
explanation.definitionFit: Being on the wagon is the idiom for not drinking alcohol, i.e. staying clear-headed.

clue.text: Does it pan out where diggers are found?

indicators.note: out signals the letters are scrambled, as in a puzzle worked out

parts.note: the nine letters rearranged

explanation.surface: Gold prospectors wonder whether panning will pay off where the miners dig.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Diggers' looks like miners, but it is slang for Australian (and New Zealand) soldiers.
explanation.definitionFit: Australia and New Zealand are the lands on the opposite side of the globe, home of the 'digger'.

clue.text: Cramped spaces are fine in small numbers

indicators.note: the word for fine sits inside the short form for numbers

parts.note: NOS is the abbreviation of numbers, 'small' showing it is shortened
OK means fine or all right

explanation.surface: Tight corners are acceptable when only a few people use them.
explanation.definitionFit: Small recesses or corners are cramped spaces, a close synonym.

clue.text: Lived as desired, after a revolution

indicators.note: a revolution overturns order, so the word's letters are turned into a new sequence

parts.note: the seven letters rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone lived just as they wished once the uprising succeeded.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After a revolution' sounds political but signals the anagram of DESIRED.
explanation.definitionFit: To have lived somewhere is to have dwelt or made one's home there.

clue.text: Either message shows who might carry it

indicators.note: the letters are on display within the two clue words, spanning them

explanation.surface: A puzzle about which of two messages identifies the courier.
explanation.walkthrough: The god sits across 'eitHER MESsage'; 'it' in the definition refers back to the message.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth the god was messenger of the Olympians, so he would carry a message.

clue.text: Émigré needs English vote backing strike

parts.note: X is the mark made on a ballot paper

indicators.note: backing here means going backwards, so the word for strike is read in reverse

parts.note: to tap is to strike lightly

explanation.surface: A emigrant must vote in favour of industrial action.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Backing' looks like support for the strike, but it turns TAP round.
explanation.definitionFit: An émigré lives abroad, away from their native country, which is what the short form of expatriate means.

clue.text: Possibly releases a French victim on Sunday

parts.note: UN is French for a
a butt is the target or victim of jokes

explanation.surface: A Frenchman falls victim to something on a Sunday.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Possibly' marks the definition as an example: undoing fastenings is one way of releasing.
explanation.definitionFit: Undoing the fastenings of a coat frees or releases it, one possible kind of releasing.

clue.text: Essential to take boat west to spot the beaver

indicators.note: the word for essential takes the other piece inside it

parts.note: must means essential, as in 'a must'

indicators.note: in an across clue going west is right to left, so the vessel's name is read backwards

parts.note: the ark is Noah's boat

explanation.surface: A nature-watcher must paddle west to catch sight of a beaver.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is loose: the muskrat is a beaver-like aquatic rodent, sometimes called a musk beaver.
explanation.definitionFit: This North American aquatic rodent resembles a small beaver and lives in lodges by the water.

clue.text: Retired, being embarassed about the act

indicators.note: the colour word goes round the other piece, enclosing it

parts.note: an embarrassed person goes red
a pose is an act put on for show

explanation.surface: Someone retired from the scene, ashamed of their performance.
explanation.definitionFit: Retired in the sense of lay down or rested, as one rests in bed.

clue.text: Starts, oddly, with a year-old goat

indicators.note: take the odd-numbered letters, first, third and fifth, of the word

explanation.surface: Something about a yearling goat starting up strangely.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Year-old goat' reads as a young animal, but 'year' gives YR and 'old goat' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: An old goat is a lecherous man; the mythical goat-legged woodland spirit is a byword for lust.

clue.text: Full of anti-oxidants?

parts.note: health-food language reinterpreted: something treated so it resists oxidation of iron or steel

explanation.surface: A question about a superfood rich in antioxidants.
explanation.walkthrough: Antioxidants suggest diet, but corrosion of iron is oxidation, so protection against it fits.
explanation.definitionFit: Metal treated to resist corrosion is protected against oxidation, playfully full of anti-oxidants.

clue.text: Ringleader clearly not a Royalist

definitions.meaning: the top of a ring is circular: a ring's head is round
a Parliamentarian in the English Civil War, opposed to the Cavaliers

explanation.surface: The leader of a gang is plainly no supporter of the king.
explanation.walkthrough: Roundheads were the Parliamentarian side in the English Civil War, named for their short haircuts.
explanation.definitionFit: Supporters of Parliament against Charles I were nicknamed for cropped hair, the Royalists' enemies.

clue.text: Part of London bus also overlooked from the bridge

definitions.meaning: the top level of a double-decker
on a ship, the highest deck is what the captain's bridge looks down on

explanation.surface: Part of a London bus can be seen from a bridge over the road.
explanation.walkthrough: The bridge here is a ship's command bridge, not a road bridge.
explanation.definitionFit: Both a double-decker bus and a ship have a top level, the higher of their decks.

clue.text: Short parallel lines, in pairs, symbolically

definitions.text: Short parallel lines, in pairs, symbolically

parts.words: Short parallel lines, in pairs, symbolically
parts.note: a mathematical symbol drawn as two short horizontal strokes, one above the other

explanation.surface: A description of a pattern of short lines drawn in pairs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Symbolically' points to maths: two short parallel dashes make the symbol for equality.
explanation.definitionFit: The symbol showing equality in arithmetic is two short horizontal parallel strokes.

clue.text: Litmus paper eg to peel off after examination

indicators.note: after puts the word for peel off behind the word for examination

parts.note: a test is an examination
to strip is to peel off, as with clothes or paint

explanation.surface: A chemist peels a litmus strip away once the experiment is done.
explanation.definitionFit: Litmus paper is one example of a chemically treated strip used to check acidity.

clue.text: Juliet's last embrace means so much more

indicators.note: only the final letter of the name is taken

parts.note: to enfold is to embrace or wrap round

explanation.surface: Juliet's final embrace of Romeo means a great deal more.
explanation.definitionFit: Multiplied by ten is a great deal more, the sense of something increased so much.

clue.text: Arab gets Skoda's first German car

indicators.note: only the opening letter of the Czech car maker's name is used

parts.note: Audi is a German car manufacturer

explanation.surface: An Arab motorist trades a Skoda for a German car.
explanation.definitionFit: A native of Saudi Arabia is an Arab by nationality and ethnicity.

clue.text: This girl is a beauty, we're told

indicators.note: said aloud, so what matters is how the phrase sounds

parts.note: a belle is a beauty, so the phrase is 'is a belle'

explanation.surface: Someone praises a girl's good looks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Is a belle' spoken runs together into the girl's name.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer is a female given name, so it names a girl.

clue.text: Enter quickly (without directions) to obtain skittle

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside: the phrase goes round the compass points

parts.note: to nip in is to enter quickly
N and E, north and east, are compass directions

explanation.surface: Instructions to dash in, ignoring directions, to get hold of a skittle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without' looks like 'lacking' but means outside: NIP IN goes around NE.
explanation.definitionFit: Each of the pins knocked down in the game of ninepins is a skittle.

clue.text: Smart leaders of new industries fire their yesmen

indicators.note: the leaders are the first letters of each following word

explanation.surface: Clever bosses of new businesses sack their sycophants.
explanation.definitionFit: Smart in the sense of clever or neat and handy, a close synonym.

clue.text: Old language in code starting with next letter

indicators.note: the opening letter is swapped for the one following it in the alphabet

parts.note: Morse is the telegraph code of dots and dashes

explanation.surface: An ancient tongue written in a cipher that begins with the next letter.
explanation.walkthrough: M is replaced by N, the next letter of the alphabet.
explanation.definitionFit: The medieval tongue of Scandinavia, Old Norse, is an old language.

clue.text: RAF tale about a dangerous carrier

indicators.note: about signals the letters are moved round into a new order

parts.note: the seven letters rearranged

explanation.surface: An air force story about a perilous aircraft carrier.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Carrier' suggests aircraft beside RAF, but it is a disease carrier.
explanation.definitionFit: The insect that lives on rodents spreads plague, so it is a dangerous carrier of disease.

clue.text: Saw a risk for trapeze artist when climbing

indicators.note: in a down clue climbing means read from bottom to top, so the phrase goes backwards

parts.note: performing with no net is a risk for a trapeze artist

explanation.surface: Someone saw how dangerous it was for an acrobat to climb.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Saw' looks like a past tense but is the noun: a tenon saw is a fine woodworking saw.
explanation.definitionFit: A tenon saw, often just called by its first word, is a short stiff-backed woodworking saw.

clue.text: Found. initially, in no doubt — then lost

indicators.note: the letter goes inside the phrase meaning no doubt

parts.note: of course means certainly, no doubt

indicators.note: only the opening letter of the word is taken

explanation.surface: Someone was found, certainly, then lost again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Found' looks like the opposite of the definition but supplies just its F.
explanation.definitionFit: A ship or traveller who has strayed from the planned route is lost.

clue.text: Green bottled water makes a comeback

indicators.note: coming back means returning, so the brand name is read backwards

parts.note: Evian is a brand of bottled mineral water

explanation.surface: Environmentally friendly bottled water returns to favour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Green' suggests ecology but means inexperienced.
explanation.definitionFit: Green in the sense of inexperienced or innocent, unworldly, matches the answer.

clue.text: Last Judgment, financially speaking

definitions.meaning: the biblical end of the world when all are judged
in money terms, the day accounts are settled and debts reckoned up

explanation.surface: The end of the world, described in money terms.
explanation.definitionFit: Judgement Day is the final reckoning, and in finance reckoning means settling accounts.
